title: Lawful basis in one screen
brief: 16:55. Marketing want to email four lists about the new cold chain service tonight, and they need finance to sign off the send.
role: Accounts payable, signing off marketing spend tonight
insight: Before “what shall we say?” comes “are we allowed to send it at all?”. Each list has its own answer.
teaches: Every use of personal data needs a lawful basis: consent, legitimate interest, or another one that fits
An opt out is a no. It stays a no for new products too
A bought list comes with none of the permissions you need

value.title: Cold chain launch email: which lists can we use?
body: “We want to email about the new cold chain service tonight. Four lists below, about 24,000 people in all. Can you sign off the send?”

policy.title: Veltrix marketing and privacy rules
lines: Consent must be freely given, specific and recorded. An opt out ends consent for all marketing.
Existing customers may be emailed about similar services if they were given a chance to opt out and did not (soft opt in). Every email must offer an easy opt out.
We do not email bought lists.

sections.title: Trade show visitors who left a business card and ticked “send me product news”

options.label: Yes: they gave consent for exactly this, with an opt out in the email
options.why: Specific, recorded consent for product news.

options.label: No
options.why: They asked for it. Refusing does not protect anyone.

sections.title: Past customers who unticked marketing at checkout

options.label: No: they said no
options.why: An opt out is an opt out, whatever the product.

options.label: Yes, it is a new service, so their no does not apply
options.why: A “no” to marketing covers new products as well.

sections.title: 20,000 logistics managers bought from a data broker, LeadHarbour

options.label: No: they never agreed to hear from us, and we cannot prove the source
options.why: Consent given to someone else is not consent to you.

options.label: Yes, the broker says the list is compliant
options.why: The broker's word does not give you a lawful basis. Your policy bans it outright.

sections.title: Customers who bought in the last year and did not opt out

options.label: Yes: a similar service, and an easy opt out in every email
options.why: The soft opt in: existing customers, similar products, a chance to say no each time.

options.label: No, we would need fresh consent
options.why: Not needed for similar services, provided the opt out is there.

messages.text: Hi Sam, the launch lists are in your Work queue. Any chance of a sign off tonight?

replies.text: Where did each list come from, and what did people agree to?

choices.label: Marketing want to email four lists. How do I decide?

script.say: List by list. Did they agree to it, or are they customers who can opt out of something similar? Opt outs stay out, and bought lists never go in.

setup.title: Work queue
setup.body: Marketing need a sign off on four email lists

outcome.label: Asked data protection
outcome.what: List by list: agreed, soft opt in, opted out, or bought.
outcome.ideal: checks the lawful basis before signing off.

outcome.label: Asked where each list came from
outcome.what: The source and what people agreed to decide whether you can send.
outcome.ideal: asks where data came from before using it.

message.text: Trade show sign ups, our checkout lists, and a list we bought from LeadHarbour last week. It says GDPR compliant on their site?

decide.objective: Decide which lists Marketing can email.
decide.insight: Consent given to someone else is not consent to you. A no stays a no.

hint.text: Ask Grace on the company chat where each list came from. In the Work queue decide list by list: the trade show sign ups and recent customers yes, the opted out and the bought list no. Data protection is on 4120.

outcome.label: Signed off only the lists with a lawful basis
outcome.what: Trade show sign ups and recent customers get the email. The opt outs and the bought list do not.
outcome.ideal: decides the lawful basis list by list.

card.title: Allowed to send, and to whom
body: People who asked for product news, and customers who can opt out of similar offers, can be emailed. People who said no, and a list bought from a broker, cannot.
Getting this right is what lets marketing send at all.
card.ideal: matches every list to a lawful basis before sending.

outcome.label: Emailed people who opted out
outcome.what: Thousands of people who said no got marketing anyway. Complaints to the regulator follow.
outcome.ideal: treats an opt out as final.

card.title: They said no
body: Customers who unticked marketing did not agree to hear about new services either. Emailing them is unlawful, and it is the fastest way to lose their trust.
card.ideal: keeps opt outs out of every campaign.

outcome.label: Emailed a bought list
outcome.what: 20,000 people who never heard of Veltrix got marketing from it. The broker's “compliant” label protects nobody.

card.title: Someone else's permission
body: Consent given to a broker, if it was ever given, is not consent to Veltrix. You also cannot show where the data came from, which you must be able to do.
card.ideal: only emails people with a basis you can prove.

outcome.label: Blocked lists that could have been used
outcome.what: Safe, but over cautious: people who asked for the news, or recent customers, would have been fine to email.
outcome.ideal: knows when the law does allow sending.

card.title: Safe, but too strict
body: Nothing unlawful went out, but some lists had a perfectly good basis. Privacy rules are there to decide, not only to refuse. Open the case to see which.
card.ideal: allows what has a lawful basis, and blocks what does not.
